successor: Kalachuris of Tripuri (Karna), then Varman (Yadava-Varman) dynasty
source1: Unsigned online transcription of the Kalachuris of Tripuri introduction, Inscriptions of the Kalachuri-Chedi Era Part 1 (apparently V.V. Mirashi, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum IV, ASI 1955) - https://www.whatisindia.com/inscriptions/kalachuri-chedi/kalachuri-chedi-part1/kalachurioftripuri28.html
source2: A.M. Chowdhury, 'Chandra Dynasty, The' and 'Varman Dynasty', Banglapedia, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Chandra_Dynasty,_The ; https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Varman_Dynasty
notes: A Chola raid c.1021-24 weakened Govindachandra. Kalachuri Karna (external, central India) overthrew the Chandra king of Vanga before 1048-49 and placed Vajravarman in charge, and the Varmans then ruled Vikramapura. Banglapedia hedges ('possibly'). Ganga candidate is Orissa, not core.

source2: Muzeum Historii Polski (Museum of Polish History), 'The Union of Lublin', polishhistory.pl, 2019 - https://polishhistory.pl/?p=514
notes: Union of Lublin (1 July 1569), bargained in parallel Polish and Lithuanian Sejms, turned the dynastic union into one federated state with a joint Sejm and elected king. Crown apparatus and king continued despite prior coercive annexations. Alternative: S3/T0.

successor: Oneota and later Illinois groups (after a gap)
source1: L.V. Benson, T.R. Pauketat, E.R. Cook, 'Cahokia's Boom and Bust in the Context of Climate Change', American Antiquity 74(3), 2009 - https://www.usgs.gov/publications/cahokias-boom-and-bust-context-climate-change
source2: A.J. White, S.E. Munoz, S. Schroeder, L.R. Stevens, 'After Cahokia: Indigenous Repopulation and Depopulation of the Horseshoe Lake Watershed AD 1400-1900', American Antiquity 85(2), 2020 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/C678D62BE9FAB07C9283D62BE9757685/core-reader
notes: Archaeological phase with no recorded central authority. Cahokia and much of the central Mississippi valley were abandoned by c.1350, with the population minimum c.1400. Culturally distinct Oneota-related and Illinois groups repopulated the area after 1500. Database end 1400 is late.

source2: Tara Prakash, 'Egypt in the Old Kingdom (ca. 2649-2130 B.C.)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/egypt-in-the-old-kingdom-ca-2649-2150-b-c
notes: Late Old Kingdom decentralisation: provincial governors became autonomous, central authority weakened, the throne passed to Herakleopolitan kings (internal) and a rival Theban line divided Egypt. No foreign conquest. Sources date the end c.2130-2118 BCE, against the database's 2150.

source1: C.A. Peterson, 'Court and province in mid- and late T'ang', in D. Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China vol. 3, Cambridge University Press 1979 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/CBO9781139055949A011/type/BOOK_PART
notes: The An Lushan rebellion (755-763) took Chang'an and An tried but failed to replace the Tang. The Tang court continued to 907 with more independent provinces, so 763 is a period break. Database successor text 'Later Tang' (923-937) is wrong.

successor: British Uganda Protectorate (Bito kings as subordinate rulers)
source2: Shane Doyle, Crisis and Decline in Bunyoro: Population and Environment in Western Uganda 1860-1955, James Currey/British Institute in Eastern Africa 2006 - https://boydellandbrewer.com/9780852554319
notes: Bito dynasty of Bunyoro-Kitara. British forces invaded in 1893-94, deposed Kabalega in 1894, broke resistance by 1899 and absorbed the kingdom into the protectorate in 1896. Q4 Y: Kabalega's 1869-70 succession war. Bito rule began well before the database's 1700.

successor: Kingdom of Hawaii under Kamehameha II
source2: Emma Chapman, 'Queen Ka'ahumanu', U.S. National Park Service, 2022 - https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/queen-ka-ahumanu.htm
notes: Kamehameha I died in May 1819. His son Liholiho succeeded as Kamehameha II, with Ka'ahumanu as kuhina nui, and the same kingdom continued, so 1819 is a period break. Q4 Y: the unification wars of 1782-1795.

source1: Parvathi Menon, 'The Carnatic Debts and the Agrarian Crisis of the Eighteenth Century', Review of Agrarian Studies, Foundation for Agrarian Studies - https://ras.org.in/articles/202/text/article.html
source2: John Clark Marshman, History of India vol. 2, ch. 20 'Lord Wellesley's Administration continued, 1799-1802' (1867) - https://ibiblio.org/britishraj/Marshman2/chapter20.html
notes: A Company client state. After Umdat ul-Umara died (1801) the Company set aside his heir, installed Azim-ud-Daula and took the civil and military government by treaty, with no battle. Q4 Y: the 1749-54 succession war. The capital was then Madras.

successor: Quanrong, then Qin (Zhou court continued at Luoyi as Eastern Zhou)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'China: The Zhou dynasty' (excerpt at Youwang entry) - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Youwang
notes: In 771 invading tribes (Quanrong, allied with Shen) killed King You and sacked Hao. The court relocated east, and the Wei-valley core passed to the Rong and then Qin. Zhou kingship survived elsewhere. The 1122 start date is traditional (c.1046).

Charlemagne invaded in 773 and Pavia, the royal seat at the end, fell after a year's siege. Desiderius was captured and Charlemagne became king of the Lombards. The listed capitals (Verona; Milan) are wrong. Q4 Y: 756-57 Ratchis-Desiderius succession contest.
